title: E0046: Input-Controlled Cardinality
plain_english: This rule reports request-controlled values that reach loops, allocation sinks, or callees without a bound. Cardinality is separate from taint: a value may be tainted without controlling collection size, and an input-controlled collection may contain ordinary strings.
why_matters: When user input controls how many times code loops or how much memory is allocated, a large or unexpected value can cause excessive CPU use, memory growth, or denial of service. Adding an explicit bound or validation step makes the cost predictable.
bad_example:
<?php
function loadAll(PDO $db): array
{
    return $db->query('SELECT * FROM users')->fetchAll(); // unbounded
}
good_example:
<?php
function loadPage(PDO $db, int $limit, int $offset): array
{
    $stmt = $db->prepare('SELECT * FROM users LIMIT ? OFFSET ?');
    $stmt->execute([$limit, $offset]);
    return $stmt->fetchAll();
}
what_it_checks: Request-relevant `$_SERVER` keys such as `HTTP_*`, `REQUEST_*`, `PHP_AUTH_*`, `QUERY_STRING`, and `PATH_INFO`; iterating the whole `$_SERVER` array is treated as server metadata
Request-controlled values used as loop bounds
Request-controlled values passed to allocation sinks such as `str_repeat()`, `range()`, `array_fill()`, `array_pad()`, `str_split()`, `explode()`, and `preg_split()`
Request-controlled arguments passed to local functions or methods whose resource summary iterates or allocates in proportion to that argument
